title: Afghan-Style Aushak with Leeks, Tomato Sauce & Garlic Yogurt
dek: Tender leek-filled dumplings sit in a warmly spiced tomato sauce beneath cool garlic yogurt and dried mint—a practical wrapper-based route to an Afghan gathering dish with vivid hot-cold contrast.
image_alt: Afghan-style aushak leek dumplings covered with red tomato sauce, drizzled garlic yogurt and dried mint on a white platter
ingredients: 1 1/4 lb leeks (about 3 medium), white and light-green parts only, quartered lengthwise, rinsed well and cut into 1/4-inch pieces
4 scallions, thinly sliced, white and green parts separated
1/2 tsp fine sea salt, divided, plus more for the cooking water
36 square wonton wrappers (about 12 oz), thawed if frozen
1 tbsp all-purpose flour mixed with 2 tbsp water, for sealing
1/4 tsp crushed red pepper, plus more to taste
1 tsp granulated sugar, optional, if the tomatoes taste sharp
3 tbsp water, plus more as needed
2 tbsp chopped fresh cilantro, for serving

instructions.name: Sweat the leek filling until dry
instructions.text: Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a wide skillet over medium. Add the leeks, scallion whites, coriander, 1/4 teaspoon salt and black pepper. Cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until tender and no liquid remains in the pan. Stir in the scallion greens for 30 seconds, spread the mixture on a plate and cool for 15 minutes. A dry, cool filling is essential for wrappers that seal instead of splitting.

instructions.name: Build the spiced tomato sauce
instructions.text: While the filling cools, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil in a medium saucepan over medium. Add the onion and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until soft. Add half of the minced garlic, the cumin, turmeric and crushed red pepper; stir for 30 seconds. Add the tomatoes, 1/2 cup water and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Simmer uncovered over medium-low for 18 to 22 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thick enough to leave a brief trail when stirred. Taste and add the sugar only if needed. Keep warm over low heat.

instructions.name: Mix the cool garlic yogurt
instructions.text: Whisk the yogurt, remaining minced garlic, lemon juice and 3 tablespoons water until smooth and pourable. Add another teaspoon or two of water if needed for a thick drizzle. Cover and refrigerate while the dumplings are shaped so the yogurt stays cool and the garlic mellows.

instructions.name: Fill and seal 36 dumplings
instructions.text: Keep the wonton wrappers under a barely damp towel. Place one wrapper like a diamond on the work surface and add 2 level teaspoons cooled leek filling to the center. Brush the edges lightly with the flour slurry, fold the bottom point to the top to form a triangle and press firmly around the filling to expel air. Bring the two side points together and seal with a dab of slurry. Arrange under a second barely damp towel and repeat. Do not stack the uncooked dumplings.

instructions.name: Prepare the serving platter
instructions.text: Spread about one-third of the warm tomato sauce across a large warmed platter. Spoon one-third of the garlic yogurt over the sauce. This base cushions the cooked wrappers and seasons their undersides without leaving them in plain cooking water.

instructions.name: Boil in calm batches
instructions.text: Bring a wide pot of well-salted water to a gentle boil. Cook the dumplings in three batches of 12, stirring once immediately so they do not stick. After they float, cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, until the wrappers are tender and translucent at the seams, 4 to 5 minutes total. Lift each batch with a wide slotted spoon and drain for several seconds; avoid tipping them into a colander, which can tear the hot wrappers.

instructions.name: Layer the aushak while hot
instructions.text: Arrange each drained batch in a slightly overlapping layer on the sauced platter. Spoon the remaining warm tomato sauce over and around the dumplings, leaving a few edges visible. Drizzle with the remaining cool garlic yogurt in broad ribbons, matching the finished dish in the photograph.

instructions.name: Finish with mint and serve
instructions.text: Rub the dried mint between your palms over the platter and scatter on the cilantro. Rest for 3 minutes so the sauces settle without making the wrappers soggy, then serve six dumplings per person. Pass extra crushed red pepper separately.

why_it_works: Cooking the leeks until their pan is dry concentrates their sweetness and prevents steam or vegetable water from weakening the wrapper seams.
Cooling the filling before shaping protects the thin wrappers; warm filling makes them sticky, fragile and difficult to seal around trapped air.
A gentle boil cooks the wrapper through without battering the filled dumplings against the pot, while a slotted spoon supports them better than a colander.
Tomato sauce goes beneath and above the dumplings, seasoning both sides while keeping the hot wrappers from sticking to the serving platter.
Cool tart yogurt balances the warm tomato sauce, and blooming dried mint only in the steam above the finished platter preserves its fresh aroma.
swaps: If gandana, the long mild allium traditionally used for aushak, is available, replace the leeks and scallions with 1 pound cleaned gandana and cook it by the same visual cues.
Round dumpling wrappers can replace square wonton wrappers. Fold them into half-moons and use about 2 teaspoons filling so the dough-to-filling ratio stays balanced.

For a meat-topped variation, brown 8 ounces lean ground beef or lamb after the onion, cook it to 160°F, then add the spices and tomatoes. The photographed version and this base recipe use tomato sauce without meat.
Regular whole-milk yogurt can replace Greek yogurt; omit the added water and whisk until pourable. A thick unsweetened dairy-free yogurt also works, though its acidity and consistency vary by brand.
Fresh mint can replace dried mint for a greener flavor. Use 1 tablespoon finely chopped leaves and add them with the cilantro rather than rubbing them between your palms.
storage: Aushak is best just after assembly because dressed wrappers continue to absorb sauce. Refrigerate leftovers in a shallow airtight container within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat covered in a 325°F oven for 15 to 20 minutes, or microwave in short intervals, until the center reaches 165°F; add a fresh spoonful of cold yogurt after reheating. Freeze uncooked dumplings in one layer until firm, then bag for up to 1 month and boil from frozen for 1 to 2 extra minutes. Freeze tomato sauce separately for up to 2 months; do not freeze the yogurt sauce.
notes: Leeks hide grit between their layers. Quarter them first, rinse under running water while separating the leaves, then drain and cut; washing only the intact stalk is not enough.
Wonton wrappers dry quickly. Keep both the unused wrappers and shaped dumplings under barely damp towels, but do not let wet cloth touch the dough or the surfaces can become gummy.
The flour slurry is more reliable than plain water for packaged wrappers. Brush a thin film only on the rim—puddles make the seams slide instead of bond.
If a wrapper tears during shaping, transfer its filling to a fresh wrapper. If one splits in the pot, remove it before loose filling clouds the water and lower the boil before continuing.
Calories and cost are estimates for six dumplings plus both sauces. Wrapper brand, leek size and yogurt prices cause the largest variation.

faqs.q: What is the difference between aushak and mantu?
faqs.a: Aushak are usually filled with gandana or another mild allium, then boiled and served with yogurt and a savory sauce. Afghan mantu are generally filled with seasoned meat and onion and steamed. Both are layered dumpling dishes, but their filling and cooking method create distinct textures and flavors.

faqs.q: Can I shape the dumplings ahead of time?
faqs.a: Shape them up to 4 hours ahead, dust a parchment-lined tray very lightly with flour, arrange them without touching and refrigerate under plastic wrap. For longer storage, freeze the tray immediately and bag the firm dumplings. Do not refrigerate them overnight; the leek moisture eventually softens packaged wrappers.

faqs.q: Why did my aushak open while boiling?
faqs.a: The filling may have been warm or wet, air may have remained around it, or the pot may have been boiling too hard. Cool the cooked leeks completely, use only 2 level teaspoons per wrapper, press outward around the mound before sealing and maintain a gentle rather than rolling boil.
